title: Mark Zuckerberg Wanted AI to Replace Meta Workers- Plan Collapsed Within Months
content:
Mark Zuckerberg Reportedly Wanted AI to Replace Meta Workers. The Plan Collapsed Within Months.
The initiative, code-named "Project OT," for Organization Transformation, envisioned turning Meta into an "AI native" company.
Mark Zuckerberg entered 2026 with an ambitious plan to remake Meta around artificial intelligence, potentially eliminating or reassigning thousands of jobs as AI agents took over work once performed by employees. Within months, however, the strategy was encountering employee resistance, security problems, and evidence that the technology was not delivering the productivity gains executives had expected.
A Reuters special report, based on scores of internal documents, recordings and interviews with more than 20 people familiar with the company's operations, revealed that Zuckerberg and his leadership team developed the initiative during a January retreat at his Hawaii compound.
The initiative, code-named "Project OT," for Organization Transformation, envisioned turning the Facebook and Instagram parent into an "AI native" company. Under the most aggressive scenarios considered by executives, some Meta teams could shrink by up to 60%, with AI handling more daily tasks and smaller groups of highly productive employees overseeing the work.
Meta stressed to Reuters that the 60% figure applied only to scenarios involving certain teams and was never a plan to eliminate 60% of the company's overall workforce. Project OT was expected to unfold in two waves.
The first would take place in May and the second in November. Layoffs would be combined with eliminating open positions, redeploying workers, and removing employees considered poor performers.
But hours before the first round of layoffs on May 20, Zuckerberg abandoned plans for the second company-wide wave. Meta proceeded with a 10% workforce reduction, but Zuckerberg subsequently told remaining employees that he did "not expect other company-wide layoffs this year."
The reversal came as Meta's AI experiment was producing troubling internal results. Employees were generating far more code with AI tools, but that surge was not translating proportionally into products reaching users.
Internal data cited by the outlet showed code changes to Meta's software platforms and infrastructure increased 220% year over year, while changes resulting in new or upgraded user-facing features rose just 36%.
More concerning were reliability and security problems. Internal posts warned that AI agents were taking disruptive actions humans were unlikely to perform. Major technical and security incidents, including outages and possible data leaks, increased 40% from the previous year, while the amount of time employees spent responding to those problems jumped 70%.
Employee morale was also deteriorating. Workers became increasingly convinced they were being asked to train the systems that could eventually replace them, particularly after Meta required tracking software on U.S. employees' computers to record keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training.
Meta's internal employee sentiment score subsequently fell from 74% favorable to 55%, according to its half-year Pulse survey cited by Reuters. Employees protested internally with angry posts, jokes and images of elephants meant to symbolize layoffs as the "elephant in the room." Meta eventually paused the tracking initiative and allowed some engineers who had been transferred into new AI-focused positions to return to their previous teams.
The company's original vision went well beyond simply giving workers AI assistants. An internal "AI-Native Playbook" described replacing traditional product-development teams of 10 to 20 specialists with pods of roughly three to five people. Conventional titles could disappear in favor of a more flexible "builder" role, while layers of middle management would be removed.
Meta was simultaneously identifying what it called "Irreplaceable Talent," including hypothetical "10X Performers" capable of producing the output of much larger teams with help from AI. By July, however, Zuckerberg publicly acknowledged that a central assumption behind the overhaul had not materialized on schedule. AI agent development, he said, had not "accelerated" as quickly as anticipated.
Zuckerberg has also shifted his public message toward AI as a technology that empowers workers rather than simply replaces them. In his essay "The Future is for Everyone," he predicted an "abundance of jobs" while acknowledging that individual companies could ultimately employ fewer people.

report.summary: Zuckerberg's plan to remake Meta with AI, cutting or reassigning thousands of jobs, collapsed within months amid security issues, weak productivity gains, and employee resistance.
report.background: In January 2026, Mark Zuckerberg and Meta's leadership met at his Hawaii compound and launched 'Project OT' (Organization Transformation), aiming to turn Meta into an 'AI-native' company. The plan envisioned replacing traditional teams with small AI-agent-led pods, with the most aggressive scenarios shrinking certain teams by up to 60%. Two waves of job changes were planned for May and November. Internal data soon showed AI-generated code not translating into more user-facing features, alongside rising technical incidents and security concerns. Employee sentiment plunged after mandatory tracking software was introduced to train AI on worker behavior. By May, Zuckerberg canceled the second wave, and by July he acknowledged AI agents had not accelerated as expected, publicly pivoting to framing AI as worker empowerment.
key_points: Project OT was a two-phase overhaul: Meta planned layoffs, redeployments, and performance-based removals in May and November, with some teams potentially shrinking 60%. It favored three-to-five-person 'AI-native pods' over 10-20-person teams. Hours before the May 20 layoffs, Zuckerberg canceled the November wave and later said no more company-wide cuts were expected this year.

Internal data highlighted a productivity mismatch: code changes to Meta's platforms jumped 220% year over year, but changes that produced new or upgraded user-facing features rose just 36%. The surge in AI-assisted coding did not proportionally improve shipped products, one of the core reasons the aggressive replacement strategy lost credibility.

Reliability and security worsened during the experiment. Major technical incidents—including outages and possible data leaks—increased 40%, and time employees spent responding to them rose 70%. Internal posts warned that AI agents took disruptive actions humans would avoid, showing that autonomy without sufficient guardrails created new operational risks.

Employee morale collapsed as workers felt they were training their replacements. Meta required tracking software on U.S. employees' computers, recording keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training. Internal sentiment fell from 74% favorable to 55%. Protests, 'elephant in the room' jokes, and pushback led Meta to pause tracking and allow some engineers to return to previous roles.

Zuckerberg publicly reversed course. He admitted AI agents had not 'accelerated' as quickly as assumed, and shifted his message to AI as an empowerment tool rather than a job replacer. His essay predicted an 'abundance of jobs' while acknowledging individual companies may employ fewer people, signaling a strategic retreat from the most extreme AI-replacement vision.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's collapse is a reality check: generating more code or AI activity doesn't automatically translate into business outcomes. It shows that large-scale workforce replacement is not yet operationally viable, and that security, reliability, and human oversight remain critical. Developers should treat AI agents as collaborators requiring guardrails, observability, and performance metrics tied to shipped value, not raw activity. For regular users, the episode suggests AI-driven services may face more outages and data-risk during transition, but also that companies will likely avoid sudden automation-led cutbacks. The broader lesson is that 'AI-native' restructuring must be incremental and measured, not a sweeping proclamation.
report.tools: For those following this space, open-source agent frameworks like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and AutoGPT show how AI agents can be built and orchestrated. Meta's own Llama models remain relevant for experimenting with on-premise AI. Observability tools such as Langfuse or OpenTelemetry can help track whether AI-generated code actually ships features, while Litellm helps monitor and route calls. These are useful to test the gap between AI output and real-world reliability.
